title: How to secure autonomous enterprise AI agents in manufacturing environments
summary: Prevent shop-floor breaches and physical hazards. Learn 5 identity-first rules to secure autonomous AI agents across IT/OT manufacturing environments using short-lived tokens, mTLS, and fail-closed controls.
body_markdown:
### Key takeaways


Securing autonomous AI agents in manufacturing requires replacing static service accounts and shared credentials with identity-first Zero Trust controls. Specifically, enterprises must enforce short-lived ephemeral tokens, dual-layer "on-behalf-of" authorization, cryptographic hardware identities, automated lifecycle deprovisioning, and fail-closed architectures to prevent compromised agents from causing physical equipment damage or supply chain disruption.


## Why legacy identity models fail autonomous manufacturing agents


[AI agent security in manufacturing](https://www.okta.com/industries/manufacturing/) means applying identity-first controls—not legacy service accounts, shared machine sign-in credentials, or static API secrets—to autonomous maintenance bots, production scheduling agents, quality-inspection vision systems, and automated supply chain orchestrators that are transforming modern industrial enterprises. Unlike deterministic automation (such as traditional programmable logic controllers, fixed robotics scripts, or legacy enterprise resource planning (ERP) workflows), autonomous AI agents operate probabilistically. They parse unstructured operational telemetry, execute dynamic multi-step tasks across previously segregated information technology (IT) and operational technology (OT) networks, and trigger actions directly inside manufacturing execution systems (MES) and industrial control environments. When access models built for human engineers or simple machine-to-machine integrations are stretched to cover autonomous AI agents, the perimeter fails.


The shift toward agentic manufacturing and autonomous plant operations is accelerating at breakneck speed. Driven by skilled-labor shortages, supply chain volatility, and[the promise of Industry 4.0](https://www.okta.com/resources/whitepapers/how-manufacturers-can-reap-the-rewards-of-digital-transformation/) , manufacturers are rapidly advancing past passive predictive analytics into active operational agents. These agents do more than flag an overheating spindle bearing—they autonomously reroute assembly line traffic, adjust boiler feed rates, reorder raw components from alternative suppliers, and negotiate procurement contracts.


Yet across manufacturing, operational enthusiasm for adopting AI agents is drastically outpacing the identity and access governance needed to secure them. Plant managers, continuous improvement teams, and OT engineers are under relentless pressure to optimize yield and minimize downtime. As a result, third-party AI assistants, autonomous shop-floor copilots, and cloud-connected diagnostics agents are frequently plugged directly into production databases and supervisory control and data acquisition bridges without centralized information security or enterprise identity and access management (IAM) oversight. In manufacturing, shadow AI carries consequences far beyond data leaks: An unmonitored agent with write access to plant systems can compromise the safety of physical equipment, ruin production batches, or trigger catastrophic environmental non-compliance.


This reality has made cross-vendor operational security frameworks—anchored by initiatives like the[Blueprint Alliance](https://www.okta.com/blueprint-alliance/) —essential for manufacturing identity leaders. To secure their environments, leaders must be able to answer four critical questions: *Where are my agents? What can they connect to? What can they do? And how do I respond?*


Here are five foundational identity rules that answer those questions for manufacturing decision-makers and protect physical operations, intellectual property, and supply chain integrity.


## How do you eliminate standing privileges across IT/OT boundaries?


### Rule 1: Replace long-lived credentials with short-lived tokens


Historically, OT and industrial software architectures relied on long-lived service tokens, hardcoded database credentials, and static API keys embedded in configuration scripts to link plant-floor equipment to MES and ERP layers. Equipping an autonomous AI agent with these same persistent credentials grants it perpetual, unconstrained access across sensitive production backends. If a prompt injection or unvalidated tool use compromises an agent analyzing boiler pressure or spindle vibration, an attacker inherits standing access to critical industrial controllers.


- **Mandate dynamic token minting:** Manufacturing enterprises must mandate ephemeral, short-lived access tokens minted dynamically by a centralized identity provider.
- **Enable an instantaneous kill switch:** Strict architectural controls must prohibit static service accounts, direct long-lived OAuth grants, and unmonitored agentic connections bridging the Purdue Model layers. This helps ensure security and plant engineering teams hold a centralized, instantaneous kill switch to revoke an agent’s authority without halting unaffected plant machinery or taking entire production lines offline.


In an industrial context, this is the vital difference between severing an anomaly-detection agent's connection to an individual milling cell during irregular behavior versus allowing a hijacked static token to pivot horizontally across the enterprise network from the plant floor into proprietary computer-aided design and manufacturing (CAD/CAM) repositories.


## How do you maintain accountability when AI agents act for engineers?


### Rule 2: Enforce true, dual-layer “on-behalf-of” authorization


A prevalent shortcut in industrial AI deployments is service impersonation: allowing an AI agent to execute actions under the broad, shared privileges of a plant supervisor account or a generic administrative service profile. This practice erodes non-repudiation, masks accountability on the factory floor, and violates core least-privilege standards.


#### Bind two distinct identities


True "on-behalf-of" authorization mandates that the central authorization plane evaluate and cryptographically bind two separate identities before permitting any operational action:


- **The initiating identity:** the process engineer, plant technician, or supply chain planner requesting or configuring the task
- **The acting agent identity:** the specific AI model, versioned prompt harness, or autonomous agent executing the workflow


#### Enforce permission intersection


The granted token must strictly restrict the agent to the intersection of both identity scopes, logging both entities in every control transaction.


This constraint is critical when operations cross the IT/OT boundary. If a maintenance technician delegates work to an AI agent to recalibrate furnace temperature parameters or order replacement parts, dual-layer authorization helps ensure that the agent cannot exceed the individual technician's certified clearance levels, access hazardous recipe formulations, or modify safety thresholds outside the technician’s assigned workcell.


## How do you verify agent actions for compliance and root-cause analysis?


### Rule 3: Require cryptographic machine identity and immutable audit trails


You cannot secure, audit, or isolate an agent you cannot unambiguously identify.


#### Anchor in hardware


Manufacturing enterprises must provision autonomous agents with cryptographically verifiable machine identities backed by hardware roots of trust (such as trusted platform modules or secure enclaves), mutual Transport Layer Security (mTLS), and remote attestation.


#### Log end-to-end execution


These credentials must feed into tamper-resistant, immutable audit pipelines that record every prompt interpretation, tool invocation, telemetry query, and physical execution command.


For industrial decision-makers, cryptographically backed identity and audit trails resolve stringent operational and regulatory imperatives:


- **Industrial cybersecurity standards (IEC 62443 and NIST SP 800-82):** Mandate verifiable identity controls, strict zone segmentation, and detailed non-repudiation logging across all automated entities interacting with industrial automation and control systems.
- **Intellectual property and International Traffic in Arms Regulations/CMMC protection:** In aerospace, defense, and high-tech manufacturing, proprietary CAD schematics, material formulations, and tooling designs represent core enterprise value. Verifiable identity helps ensure AI agents handling generative engineering cannot exfiltrate export-controlled technical data.
- **Batch traceability and root cause analysis:** When a chemical batch fails quality inspection or a structural weld fails stress testing, an immutable audit trail answers definitively: Which agent executed the parameter change? On whose behalf? At what exact millisecond? And using which sensor inputs?


## How do you prevent orphaned pilot agents from becoming backdoors?


### Rule 4: Automate continuous identity lifecycle management


[Least privilege](https://www.okta.com/identity-101/what-is-least-privilege-access/) in manufacturing is not a set-and-forget milestone. Plant configurations evolve continuously: production lines retool for new vehicle models, temporary third-party contractors configure pilot machinery, and dynamic production schedules demand shifting system access.


Unmonitored and abandoned agents—such as an experimental yield-optimization agent spun up during a production trial, or an autonomous inventory scraper deployed during a raw material shortage—represent glaring backdoors. Without lifecycle oversight, orphaned agents retain excessive privileges that attackers can exploit to bypass perimeter firewalls and access core programmable logic controllers and ERP tables.


Enterprise IAM teams must establish automated lifecycle guardrails tailored to industrial lifecycles:


- **Active agent discovery:** Continuous asset and agent discovery mechanisms that catalog every AI agent, tool integration, and protocol connector spanning cloud platforms, edge gateways, and on-premises shop-floor servers.
- **Automated deprovisioning and time-to-live:** Automated policies that automatically de-register credentials, revoke tool access, and sever API endpoints for agents exhibiting inactivity, decommissioned production cells, or expiring maintenance contracts.
- **Continuous behavioral attestation:** Anomaly-detection systems that monitor tool-calling frequency and data access volumes. If a predictive maintenance agent suddenly attempts to query financial accounting ledgers or exfiltrate firmware binaries, its privileges must be stepped down immediately.


## How do you prevent physical hazards during network or auth outages?


### Rule 5: Mandate fail-closed security architectures


In an autonomous environment that interfaces with kinetic machinery, interruptions to authentication, identity validation, or communication bridges should not cause an agent to default to an unconstrained, bypass state.


#### Suspend actuation on auth failure


If an agent’s authorization server, telemetry verification stream, or safety verification harness drops offline, the system must fail closed—suspending autonomous actuation and defaulting to a safe operational state rather than executing unmonitored commands.


#### Mitigate kinetic risks


The physical hazards of a fail-open architecture in manufacturing are severe:


- An autonomous chemical dosing agent that loses connection to its central policy server could continue adjusting valve positions without guardrails, risking hazardous spills or chemical thermal runaway.
- An automated guided vehicle or robotic arm agent that fails to refresh its authorization tokens could ignore updated plant-floor geofencing constraints, posing an imminent danger to human workers sharing the facility floor.


By enforcing fail-closed mechanisms at the identity and policy enforcement layers, industrial enterprises can help ensure that unexpected network interruptions or security outages translate into a controlled, fail-safe operational pause rather than physical asset damage, human injury, or regulatory fines.


## How do AI agent identity risks differ across manufacturing sectors?


The implementation of these five rules directly addresses the unique operational risks of major manufacturing sectors.


Manufacturing sector Primary agent use cases Critical identity control Prevented operational failure


Discrete manufacturing (automotive, industrial, electronics) Automated line balancing, robotic weld/torque calibration Dual-layer on-behalf-of authentication and strict role boundaries Unauthorized overrides of calibrated assembly tolerances without engineer sign-off


Process manufacturing (chemicals, pharmaceuticals, oil, and gas) Autonomous recipe adjustment, boiler and valve control Fail-closed architecture and cryptographic identity Unmonitored pressure/temperature changes causing batch contamination or spills


Supply chain and logistics (procurement, warehousing, distribution) Autonomous purchase order execution, vendor onboarding, warehouse fulfillment Short-lived tokens and continuous lifecycle governance Vendor impersonation, invoice fraud, and unauthorized inventory reallocation


## Building the foundation for trustworthy industrial AI


Autonomous AI agents represent the future of agile, highly efficient, and self-optimizing manufacturing. However, unlocking this industrial productivity requires discarding brittle, static service credentials in favor of centralized visibility, cryptographic machine identities, dynamic short-lived tokens, and fail-closed safety designs.
